episode_title: How I Would Market A Financial Advisor With Only $10,000

real_qa.q: How would you allocate a $10,000 marketing budget as a financial advisor starting from scratch with no clients or audience?
real_qa.r: Start with niche selection ($0), then allocate $500 for copywriting education, $1,200 for a client-getting website, $600 for email software for one year, $1,500 for direct mail campaigns, $400 for CRM software, $2,388 for ongoing education like an inner circle newsletter, and keep $3,412 in cash reserve to double down on what works after 90 days of testing.

real_qa.q: What is the difference between buying marketing assets versus renting marketing results?
real_qa.r: Every marketing dollar either buys you an asset or rents you a result. When you buy ads, you are renting attention that stops the day you stop paying. When you buy leads, you are renting names that have been sold to multiple advisors. When you build an email list or publish owned content, you own it and it keeps producing clients after you stop paying. Assets keep producing after you stop feeding them money, while expenses produce something only while you pay.
real_qa.requete: marketing assets versus renting results financial advisors

real_qa.q: Why should financial advisors avoid buying leads for client acquisition?
real_qa.r: When you buy a lead, you are buying a name that has been sold to multiple financial advisors, and you enter that relationship as a commodity. These prospects are comparison shopping, they don't know you, they don't trust you, and you are the fourth voicemail on their phone that week. You start from a position of weakness instead of building a relationship where you own the prospect.
real_qa.requete: why buying leads is bad financial advisors

real_qa.q: How does the effort heuristic principle apply to financial advisor direct mail marketing?
real_qa.r: In 2004, Justin Kruger and colleagues published research showing that people consistently rate high-effort items as better and more valuable than quick efforts. A physical letter addressed to a specific prospect carries perceived effort and value, while LinkedIn messages take 11 seconds and carry no perceived effort. Meanwhile, the physical mailbox is emptier than it has been in decades with less competition, so direct mail combines less competition with more perceived effort—a wonderful combination.
real_qa.requete: effort heuristic direct mail marketing 2004 Kruger research

real_qa.q: Why is holding cash in reserve the most investor-like move in a $10,000 marketing budget?
real_qa.r: After running your marketing system for 90 days, you learn what works. If direct mail is booking appointments like crazy, you have cash to triple the mailing list. If emails are converting but your website is not, you have money to fix the actual constraint. The advisor who spends everything on day one has zero ability to double down on what works, and doubling down on what works is where all the returns are going to live.
real_qa.requete: cash reserve marketing budget double down what works

key_stats: 8 out of 10 financial advisors would waste a $10,000 marketing budget because they spend like consumers instead of investors
With a 30% performance underperformance, a $10,000 budget represents a $3,000 mistake while a $100,000 budget represents a $30,000 mistake
Direct mail cost: approximately $1 per mailing plus $1 per rented recipient name, totaling $2 per mailer, allowing 750 mailings with a $1,500 budget
Niche selection is a $0 line item that multiplies the return on every dollar that comes after it
Kit email software costs $390 per year for 1,000 email subscribers; Drip costs $400 per year for up to 2,500 email subscribers
In 2004, Justin Kruger and colleagues published research on the effort heuristic demonstrating perceived effort carries value
Financial advisors' stock portfolios grow at a much lower rate than the average
